en: The First Chapter of the *Nītiprakāśikā* composed by Vaiśampāyana.
Having bowed to the illustrious Gajānana (Gaṇeśa), Vāṇī (Sarasvatī), and the true gurus beginning with Brahmā;
This *Nītiprakāśikā* is indeed being composed by me with great reverence.
Desiring to see King Janamejaya, who was seated upon an excellent throne in the illustrious city of Takṣaśilā, [I approached him], a man of great asceticism.
The great sage named Vaiśampāyana, a disciple of Vyāsa who was firm in his vows, arrived accompanied by his disciples;
having heard that the Ṛṣi was approaching, King Janamejaya [prepared for him].
He went out to meet him suddenly, accompanied by his ministers and family priest;
having offered water for the feet, the guest-offering, a cow, and the honey-mixture according to the rite,
he spoke of his welfare with a joyful heart.
"I am blessed, I am graced, since you have come into my sight;
all my ancestors have been delivered and I myself have been protected by you, O Sage.
To the king who had spoken thus, he bestowed auspicious blessings.
Having said, "May your mind delight in the Dharma," he then went to the assembly hall.
When that sage was seated upon the auspicious throne, the best of kings sat down near his seat, surrounding him with palms joined in reverence.
Then, having reached the end of that discourse, King Janamejaya bowed with devotion to the seer and, with palms joined in reverence, spoke:
"All the duties of kings belonging to the Bharatas have been recounted by you."

I have a certain doubt in my heart; you ought to sever it for me. (10) Furthermore, O Brahmin, through the passage of time and the influence of the Kali age, dharma, truth, purity, forgiveness, and compassion daily decline, as do lifespan, strength, and memory. (11)
In the Kali age, wealth alone is the cause for men's birth, conduct, and the arising of virtues; indeed, force alone is the cause for the administration of dharma and justice.
In marriage, mutual desire is the cause; in worldly dealings, it is merely illusion.
Delight in skill regarding the female and male genders, and the Sūtra itself regarding the state of being a Brahmin;
the very gender-signs are the cause for falling into one another’s conditions during the proclamation of the stages of life (āśrama).
Through lack of livelihood comes weakness in justice; and in scholarship, there is the fickleness of speech.

In the case of "correctness," it is simply incurability; in the case of "adornment," it is merely bathing; in the case of "marriage," it is merely acceptance; in the case of "beauty," it is merely the maintenance of hair; "self-interest" is merely being full-bellied; and the "practice of dharma" for the sake of fame is merely [a hollow pretense].
Skillfulness in maintaining a household is indeed nothing but audacity in the face of truth.
For when the castes consist mostly of Śūdras, when cows are like goats, when Dharma abounds in heresy, and when kings are mostly robbers— (16–17)
"How shall this system of theirs, along with the discernment of the science of archery and the knowledge of hand-to-hand and projectile weapons, be brought under my control in its full detail?
Having heard those words, the great Ṛṣi, who knew their inner hearts, [replied].
With words imbued with meaning, he spoke thus to the king:
"Your intention has been understood by me regarding the awakening to subtle policy;
for one who has received an inquiry should explain the scripture, lest there be regret."
Brahmā, Maheśvara, Skanda, Indra, Prācetasa Manu, Bṛhaspati, Śukra, Bhāradvāja of great asceticism,
the blessed Vedavyāsa, and likewise the sage Gauraśiras.
For these were the authors of the treatises on statecraft (rājaśāstra), O scorcher of foes.
The high-minded Brahmā recited one hundred thousand chapters in the science of kings;
Rudra, having condensed it, spoke fifty thousand verses.
Vāsava, having abridged it, spoke twenty-five thousand verses of the Skanda; then Manu, the son of Pracetas, spoke ten thousand and two thousand verses.
(24) And then he spoke six thousand verses.
Bṛhaspati indeed spoke three thousand chapters;
Kāvya, having condensed that, composed a work of one thousand chapters;
likewise, Bhāradvāja proclaimed a treatise of seven hundred chapters.
The sage Gaurāśiras also recited one hundred and five chapters;
however, the blessed and high-minded Vedavyāsa, having condensed that,
composed a treatise on ethics consisting of three hundred chapters, O high-minded one.
Having understood that the lifespan of mortals is brief due to the defects of their intellect,
I shall provide you with a mere summary of its characteristics;
O King, being attentive in mind, learn from me this treatise on statecraft.
It is said that in ancient times, Pṛthu, the son of Vena, having conquered death while protecting his subjects,
was called a *kṣatriya* by them because he protected them from injury (*kṣata-trāṇāt*); thus even his name, "Rāja," arose from the affection of the people.
The earth yielded crops without being ploughed and was a cow of plenty for the son of Vena (Pṛthu).
The Darbha grass was golden, pleasant to the touch, and enchanting; the subjects, well-covered by its blades, would rest upon them.
At that time, there was no division of kingdoms or cities;
wherever people dwelt, there the earth yielded its milk with ease.
For by that [sacrifice], the waters were held back as they were being directed toward the ocean.
The mountains yielded the way, and there was no breaking of his banner.
The king fashioned sixty thousand and sixty hundred golden elephants and gave them to the Brahmins.
The King made this entire earth adorned with jewels and gems out of gold, and he gave it to the Brahmins;
having recognized these and other virtues of that king, the Four-faced One [Brahmā]— 36.
He revealed himself and said, "I am the giver of boons.
Then, having seen Brahmā and heard those words of his,
Pṛthu was exceedingly delighted and chose that supreme boon from him.
"The science of archery (dhanurveda), consisting of four divisions along with its limbs, sub-limbs, and secret doctrines, and adorned with weapons and missiles, must be bestowed upon me by you.
O one honored by the worlds, I consider myself superior to all beings in this world. (39)
"Since you, a treasure-house consisting of the Vedas, have come into my sight"—
having spoken thus, the Creator of the World then lifted up Pṛthu, who was sinking in the ocean of milk that was bliss, with a voice in the form of a boat.
"By good fortune, this intelligence has arisen in you regarding the mastery of the science of archery;
I too have come here desiring to say this very thing to you.
Previously, the sword was created by me for the purpose of subduing the wicked."
Dwelling near one such as you, he moves about instructing the worlds. Since you alone are remembered by me as the originator of the manifestation of weapons such as the bow,
I shall therefore bestow upon you, my son, both handheld weapons (*śastra*) and missile-weapons (*astra*).
Bhṛśāśva was the son of Mānasa; he had two highly esteemed wives, Jayā and Suprabhā, both daughters of Dakṣa and possessed of great intelligence.
Jayā, having obtained boons from me, gave birth indeed to various weapons and missiles.
Furthermore, she gave birth to another fifty sons named Saṃhāras,
who were invincible, difficult to assail, and exceedingly powerful;
through their union with the deities of the mantras, their weapons attained the status of missiles (*astras*).
"O best among victors, having received the science of archery from me,
protect all your subjects with righteousness as if they were your own biological sons. You are a knower of the true principles of peace and war, and a master of the discernment of inference."
Endowed with the application of the sixfold policy and proficient in all the sciences,
you are possessed of the six royal qualities; therefore, employ the seven expedients and duly examine the fourteen factors of strength and weakness.
Then, O destroyer of enemies, having examined yourself and others,
and having thus formed alliances, always practice the eight duties, O King;
you possess eighteen among others, and fifteen within your own side.
O best of kings, having learned of the enemy’s vulnerability through three trusted spies,
you should march against him with speed once you have carefully assessed the threefold force [of the enemy]. (52–53)
O subduer of enemies, having determined the proper time and having ascertained the enemy's rear-guard, their resolve, and their potential for defeat, set out on your expedition;
O lord of the people, having made your own base firm, advance against the foes.
Exert your prowess to conquer him, and having conquered him, protect [the realm].
Your army, firmly endowed with the eight limbs and consisting of the fourfold forces,
well-led by the commanders of the troops, shall increase your power over your enemies.
Having thus instructed him, Brahmā, the teacher of the world, proceeded once more to speak in order to have him master the science of archery (Dhanurveda).
Thus ends the first chapter, titled "Instruction on the Duties of Kings," preceded by a demonstration of the connection, in the illustrious *Nītiśāstra* known as the *Nītiprakāśikā*.
Srota Dhanurveda: Second Chapter
The science of archery (Dhanurveda) has four feet, is red in color, has four faces, eight arms, and three eyes; he belongs to the Sāṅkhyāyana gotra.
In his four right arms, he holds a thunderbolt, a sword, a bow, and a discus.

In his left arms he holds the *śataghnī*, the mace, the trident, and the *paṭṭiśa*. He has a million methods as his limbs, policy as his body, mantras as his armor, withdrawal as his heart, and both weapons and missiles as his earrings.
Adorned with various leaping forms as ornaments, with tawny eyes and encircled by a garland of victory, he is said to be mounted upon a bull.
(4) I shall now proclaim this mantra, which cuts through the net of enemies.

First, having uttered the syllable *praṇava* (oṃ), then the two syllables *namaḥ*, followed by *vate* preceded by *bhaga*, one should then utter *dhaṃ* for Dhanurveda. This [mantra] is the protector of one's own army, one's own faction, and oneself. 5–6.
Having uttered "Protect me, protect me," one should then say "Devour my enemies.
Having uttered "Huṃ Phaṭ Svāhā" twice, one should then recite it.
I myself am its seer (ṛṣi), and Gāyatrī is said to be its meter (chandas).

Maheśvara is its deity; its application is for the subjugation of enemies. Having recited the mantra of thirty-two syllables for as many thousands as there are syllables, one attains perfection and overcomes one's foes.
Truth, truth, and again truth—I declare this thrice here, O son of Vena: I shall now explain the exposition of the science of archery; listen to me.
It is the released, the unreleased, and beyond that, the released-unreleased.
The four branches of the science of archery (dhanurveda) are indeed described as "discharged" (mukta), "undischarged" (amukta), and "both discharged and undischarged" (muktāmukta).
Discharged weapons are to be understood as arrows and the like; undischarged weapons are swords and the like;
while weapons that involve both the discharge and the withdrawal [of the weapon] are declared to be both discharged and undischarged.
The mantra spoken here is said to be devoid of a concluding formula (*upasaṃhāra*);
through these four quarters, the science of archery (*dhanurveda*) is revealed:
namely, the weapon (*śastra*), the missile (*astra*), the counter-missile (*pratyastra*), and the supreme missile (*paramāstra*). 13.
Some experts in the science of archery say that it has four divisions: taking up the bow, aiming, releasing, and withdrawing. Others have declared that the science of archery consists of these four.
Relying upon the first of those views, I shall describe the thirty-two varieties of weapons— both those that are released and those that are not— and herein follows the detailed sequence:
the bow, the arrow, the bhindipāla, the śakti, the club, the mallet, and the tomara.

The *nalikā*, the *laguḍa*, the *pāśa*, the *cakra*, the *dantakaṇṭaka*, and the *musuṇḍī*—these twelve are proclaimed as the varieties of the *mukta* (projectile) weapons. O King, this first quarter of the science of archery (*dhanurveda*) has thus been described to you. 17–18.
The *vajramīlī*, the axe, the *gośīrṣa*, the *asidhenukā*, the winnowing fan, the mat, the spear, the pillar, the javelin, the *pināka* bow,
19 the mace, the hammer, the plow, the pestle, and likewise the *paṭṭiśa*.
The *mauṣṭika*, the *parigha*, the *mayūkhī*, and the *śataghnikā*—
these twenty unthrown [missiles] are called the second quarter;
those weapons, both thrown and unthrown, are reckoned by you as thirty-two.
The Staff-wheel, the Dharma-wheel, and likewise the Time-wheel;
the Indra-wheel, the Trident-bearing, the Brahma-head, and Modakī (22); Śikharī, the Dharma-noose, and likewise the Varuṇa-noose.
The Pāśupata weapon, the Vāyavya, the Śuṣka and Ārdra weapons, the Śikhara weapon,
the Krauñca weapon, and the Hayaśīrṣa; those known as the Vidya and Avidya weapons,
the Gāndharva weapon, the Nandana weapon, as well as the Varṣaṇa and Śoṣaṇa weapons.
The Prasvāpana and Praśamana, the Saṃtāpana and Vilāpana,
the Madana and Mānava weapons, as well as the Tāmasa, the Saṃvarta, Mausala, Satya, Saura, and the Māyā weapon. 25.

The Tvaṣṭra-missile, the Soma-missile, the Saṃhāra-missile, and likewise the Mānasa-missile; the Nāga-missile and the Gāruḍa-missile— these four, along with the two known as the Śiva-missile and the Īśika-missile, indeed constitute the eight missiles together with their methods of withdrawal.
And I shall speak of the methods of withdrawal that follow in due order; learn them from me, for by knowing them you will neutralize the weapons released by your enemies.
They are Satyavat, Satyakīrti, Rabhasa, and Dṛṣṭa.
Pratihāratara, Avāṅmukha, Parāṅmukha,
Dṛḍhanābha, Alakṣyalakṣya, Āvila, Sunābhaka,
Daśākṣa, Śatavaktra, Daśaśīrṣa, and Śatodara. (29–30)
Dharmanābha, Mahānābha, Duṃdhunābha, Nābhaka,
Jyotiṣavimalakula, both Nairāśya and Kṛśana, Yogaṃdhara, Sanidra, and the Daitya Pramathana. (31)
Sārcirmālī, Dhṛtimālī, Vṛttimān, and likewise Rucira;
Pitrya and Saumanasa, as well as Vidhūtamakara; Karavīra, Dhanarati, Dhānya, and indeed Kāmarūpaka. (32–33)
Jṛmbhaka, Varaṇa, Mōha, Kāmaruci, Varuṇa, Sarvadamana, Saṃdhāna, and Sarvanābhaka;
[and] the Kaṅkāla weapon, the Musala weapon, the Kāpāla weapon, and the Kaṅkaṇa. 34.
O King, the Paiśāca weapon— these five are the Asura weapons; Satyavān, Sarvadamana, Kāmarūpa,
as well as Yogandhara and Alakṣya, are the destroyers of the Asura weapons.
These forty-four, along with five others who crush one another, amount to forty-nine when combined; they are indeed named after weapons. But the great son of Suprabhātā is named Sarvamocana.
"O King, this third quarter-verse of the science of archery shall be: 'By my boon, he is renowned as the supreme one who has brought all things, both liberated and unliberated, to rest.
Now I shall also speak of the mantra; listen with an attentive mind. (38-39)
The Viṣṇucakra, the Vajra weapon, the Brahmāstra, the Kālapāśaka,
the Nārāyaṇa, and the Pāśupata— these six are indestructible by other weapons; because they lack any means of destruction by their own kind, these six are liberated from [the need for] mantras.
This shall be considered the fourth quarter of the science of archery (dhanurveda).
Listen further, O sinless one; I shall tell you another distinction:
in ancient times, during the war between the gods and the asuras, the gods were defeated by the dānavas.
Unskilled in the specific arts of archery and intent on flight, they beheld the sage Dadhīci, gave him their weapons,
and quickly departed for Mandara, the best of mountains, desiring to dwell there.
Out of fear, those gods, headed by Indra, dwelt there for many years.
Dadhīci also, having taken them away from the Daityas, protected those weapons—
which served as his very arrows— by means of the power of his asceticism.
Then the gods, led by Indra, having been defeated and overwhelmed by fear, took refuge with me on Mount Mandara; they were scattered and dissolved in their terror.
Then I bestowed upon the gods the science of archery (Dhanurveda), together with its secret mysteries.
Out of a desire to favor them, [he gave] that [weapon] endowed with four feet and all its auxiliary parts.
Then, having received boons from me, those foremost of the Daityas, seeing Dadhīci set out to fight, assembled and made a request of him.
Having heard the words of those who required weapons, the best of sages,
moved by compassion, reflected upon those things that were like thorns and then spoke to them:
"O dwellers of heaven, the materials for your weapons are the bones within my body."
Having licked your weapons with the tongue of a cow and sharpened them,
take them from my body and conquer your enemies in battle;
for my own death has been foreseen in this way— there is no need for deliberation here.
"Having made this body useful for the gods, go to heaven;
having accomplished your own purpose, bestow my worlds upon me.
(52) Having heard his words, those inhabitants of heaven acted accordingly.
Because his own duty was more important, they undertook that task;
O best of kings, even the sin of killing a Brahmin entered Gomukha,
while that sage went to the eternal worlds through his satisfaction of the gods.
From that time forth, O tiger among men, people here no longer saw Gomukha in the morning, for their minds were overcome by the fault of that [act].
There were thirty-one skeletons and that one vertebra.

Thirty-two [weapons] emerged from the body of that great-souled ṛṣi. Whatever bone was situated in a particular limb of the sage, whatever form it took, from that very bone there emerged a weapon possessing that very same shape.
O King, because of his sharp nature and pride, he tormented Dadhīci;
indeed, the weapons protected by him were turned into arrows,
and thirty-two such weapons will circulate in the world.
Without the thunderbolt that sprang from the *kaśeruka* plant and was held in Indra's hand,
the gods conquered the Dānavas through the majesty of the science of archery (*dhanurveda*).
From this day forward, the bow and other weapons shall circulate in the world of mortals, taking you as their limit.
"By relying upon you, who are a knower of the science of archery (dhanurveda), the best of kings will become possessed of statesmanship through my grace; of this there is no doubt.
Thus, O child, has this majesty, which is equal to the Vedas, been told."
The origin of weapons has been told; what more do you wish to hear?
He who shall master this instruction on the science of archery (dhanurveda) composed by me for your sake shall attain all his desires.
Having heard the words of Vidhi, the highly intelligent Pārīkṣita, the son of Pṛthu, then proceeded to examine the state of being residing within his heart.
Thus ends the second chapter, titled "The Exposition on the Science of Archery," in the illustrious *Nītiśāstra* known as the *Nītiprakāśikā*.
The Third Chapter:
"O Lord of the World, homage be to you, O Master who are the refuge of all wonders! You have previously declared, 'A sword has been produced by me. (1)
When indeed was this sword produced by you, and for what reason here? Who first received this supreme sword from you?
O Lord, what has been its lineage until it reached the world of mortals?
"O Grandfather, tell me about my sword's former preceptor.
Having heard those words, the Grandfather spoke as follows:
"Where, by what cause, and how he was produced in the past."
O son of Vinatā, I shall describe to you the supreme origin of the sword;
having heard this with an attentive mind, you will attain victory everywhere. O King, when your bow is shattered and your horses are exhausted, [you shall prevail].
In battle, it is possible to protect oneself well with a sword;
even against those bearing bows, as well as those bearing maces and spears,
a single heroic wielder of the sword is capable of resisting them all.
The sword is superior to other weapons; therefore, O King, it is renowned throughout the worlds.
It was created by me in ancient times for a certain purpose.
[So too were] Hiraṇyakaśipu, Hiraṇyākṣa, and Virocana.
Śambara, Vipracitti, Prahlāda, Namuci, and Bali— these and many other Daityas and Dānavas, together with their hosts,
having transgressed the bridge of dharma, began to fight with the gods. 9–10.
Then, on a peak of the Himalayas, resplendent with various minerals,
extending for a hundred yojanas and filled with forests of flowering trees,
I indeed performed a sacrifice there for the sake of accomplishing the welfare of all the worlds.
Then, at the end of a thousand years, a marvel occurred:
the sky blazed with flames of fire, illuminating the surface of the earth,
and a being of such a nature rose up from the fire-pit, scattering fire as it emerged.
It was the color of a blue lotus, with sharp fangs, a lean belly, and a tall stature;
it was exceedingly difficult to withstand, enveloped in garlands of flames, with red eyes and a cruel roar that struck fear into all living beings. 14.
With its own exceedingly fierce radiance, it robbed the sight of the beholder;
and as it was rising up, the earth trembled,
and that great ocean, filled with massive waves and whirlpools, was agitated.
Terrible meteors fell from the sky and trees shed their branches;
seeing this, all living beings trembled again and again.
Overwhelmed by fear, the great sages, gods, and gandharvas spoke to one another.
I thought to myself: "This powerful one is indeed named Asura;
for the protection of the world and for the destruction of the enemies of the gods, he has cast off that form and now shines as a sword. Thus it was. 18–19.
Stainless and with a sharp edge, raised like the Destroyer at the end of time,
fifty finger-breadths in height and four finger-breadths in width—
this sword was then placed by me into the hand of Ṛṣabhaketa.
The destroyer of Rākṣasas, the fierce one, the preventer of unrighteousness—
having raised that [spear] which strikes fear into all enemies, Mahādeva brandished his shield like a cloud accompanied by lightning. 21–22.
Possessing great strength and prowess, he moved through various maneuvers,
cutting, piercing, crushing, lopping off, rending, and trampling his enemies;
indeed, there were thirty-two techniques involved in sword-fighting.
He displayed those variegated and swift maneuvers before the host of Daityas:
the whirling, the upward-whirling, the piercing, the side-thrust, the downward-thrust, the forward-rush, the advancing, and the surging, as well as the seizing and the releasing.
In the drawing back and joining of the feet, the revolving of the head and arms,
the binding of the noose and the feet, and likewise in the whirling on the ground;
(26) in the backward and forward throws, the falling and rising, and the leaping.
Lightness, grace, beauty, steadiness, and a firm grip—oh, these thirty-two movements for moving sideways and upwards! Having conquered the Dānavas in battle, Rudra became truly joyful. 27–28.
Then the Blessed Lord Rudra, seeing Viṣṇu standing nearby,
honored him as the protector of dharma and joyfully gave him a sword.
Viṣṇu gave it to Marīci, and the venerable Marīci likewise [gave it to his son].
Ṛṣabha gave the sword to the great seers and to Vāsava;
Mahendra gave it to the world-protectors, and the world-protectors gave it to Manu, the son of the Sun. Then they spoke to him: (30–31)
"O Lord of Creatures, for the sake of dharma and purpose, instruct with the sword whose womb is dharma those who have transgressed the bridge of dharma in this world.
Having promised "So be it," he took up that supreme sword.
He indeed set it in motion in the world through the medium of the royal lineage.
O best of kings, you too receive this sword from me and protect the subjects according to dharma, as if they were your own legitimate sons.
Kṛttikā is the lunar mansion of this sword, and Agni is its deity;
Rohiṇī is its lineage, and Rudra is its presiding divinity.
Indeed, learn from me the eight secret names of the sword.
The sword is the slayer of the Asuras, characterized by sharpness, and difficult to approach;
it is the womb of prosperity, victory itself, and likewise the garland of dharma.
Thus was it proclaimed by Rudra as the foremost among all weapons. (36–37)
Swords must always be worshipped by those skilled in combat;
indeed, those who worship the sword obtain victory and fame. This narrative, endowed with the majesty of the sword, has been told to you.
I have not told this to anyone; what more do you wish to hear?
(39) Those kings who desire to conquer their enemies and take delight in marching out for battle shall obtain victory in war if they recite this [work] which brings victory. (40)
Thus ends the third chapter, titled "The Account of the Origin of the Sword," in the *Nītiprakāśikā*, the illustrious treatise on ethics.
Chapter Four:
Having heard the words of the Self-Existent One (*Svayaṃbhū*), Pṛthu was exceedingly delighted.
Bowing down with great humility, he questioned the Lotus-born One once more:
"You have mentioned to me the thirty-two weapons, both those that are released and those that are un-released; you should describe their true nature, their colors, and their methods of application."
Thus questioned by Pṛthu, the Blessed One, who is affectionate toward his devotees,
related all of that in detail, spreading forth his glory— describing which form belongs to which deity, what their colors are, and what they are like.
Now, O great-minded one, learn of those [beings] named after their weapons.
First, I shall describe the postures of the liberated ones; understand them from me, for by knowing these, one may thus fashion the arrangement of the weapons.
O best of kings, I shall first describe the true nature of the bow,
its dimensions, its configuration, and likewise the method of its practice;
therein I shall also explain its internal subdivisions as well as the method of practicing with arrows.
The seizing of the target and the piercing of the mark are fourfold.
[The bow] has a broad neck, a slender head, a thin middle, and a well-formed back; its body is four cubits tall, bent in three places, and possesses a long tongue.
With a face formidable with fangs, reddish in hue, and a gurgling sound,
encircled by a garland of entrails and licking the corners of its mouth;
and that which was born from Kṛśāśva and others for the protection of the world during the Jayā era.
Having meditated upon that with his mind and having duly bowed to the Guru according to the prescribed rite, he should,
following the rules of archery, join the string with his right hand— not with his left— and grasp it at the middle and at the back.
Placing the left thumb on its belly and the four fingers on the back,
one should join the bowstring to the middle of the nock through the space between one's own fingers;
then, drawing it back to the ear and fixing the gaze upon the target.
When one who knows the application of the bow, having fixed the arrow-shaft, releases the arrow without seeing anything other than the target,
he is then called "one with a trained hand" (*kṛtahasta*).
In this same manner arrows should be discharged, for one must protect oneself with great effort.
Those learned in the science of archery recognize four types of targets: the immovable, the minute, the delicate, and the heavy.
The immovable consists of piercing through solid objects such as rocks; the minute consists of piercing through small objects such as gunja berries.
The breaking of a hen’s egg or a water-pot is called *sukumāraka* (gentle),
while the striking down of the bodies of demons, elephants, and the like is said to be *guru* (heavy).
Thus should the expansion of the targets be understood by those most skilled in policy.

The reconnection of the target, drawing it near and pulling it away, drawing it around and following it, as well as forming a circle; likewise, filling it out, stabilizing it, shaking it, and whirling it about.
The near-miss, the far-miss, and the strikes to the back and the middle—
these fourteen are called *valgita* (swinging) movements by those skilled in the bow.
I shall now describe the various types of bows according to their respective purposes.
The Śārṅgika bow is said to have three bends; the Vaiṇava bow is entirely curved.
The weapon known as the Vaitastika bow is made of bamboo and measures one cubit (hastaka).
The Upalotkṣepaka bow is also made of bamboo and is without a string.
That [bow] should be three cubits in height and two finger-breadths in width.
Always wearing leather arm-guards and finger-protectors, and with his quiver fastened to his back, he should practice archery; otherwise, he will be one who misses his mark.
Pratyālīḍha, ālīḍha, as well as samapada, viśāla, and maṇḍala—these are known as the five postures of archers. Armor, shoulder-protectors, breastplates, helmets, and girdles [are the equipment]. 24.
The collection of mallets and clubs, and indeed the equipment of the chariot-warrior;
moving clockwise, swiftness, moving counter-clockwise, advancing, retreating, the circular maneuver, and maintaining one's position—these are the [skills]. 25–26.
Mixing, bursting, piercing, and the paths of the chariot—these ten are recorded as the branches of the science of archery; having mastered them in this way, one becomes exceedingly merciless.
An arrow has a dark-blue, massive body and is provided with a height of two cubits.
With the paridhi, he reaches as far as the añjali-measure, and his range extends to a distance of one nalva; these two movements—whirling and hurling—are for the thick and the curved [weapons].
Having understood these divisions of movement, one should fight and conquer enemies in battle.
The *bhiṇḍivāla* [staff], however, has a curved body, a downward-pointing head, and large veins;
it is one cubit in height and its circumference is equal to the span of the hand.
Its movement consists of three revolutions followed by a discharge, preceded by the left foot. 30.
The slayer of enemies by the strike of his feet is to be supported by circles of foot-soldiers. His spear is two cubits in height, moving horizontally with composure,
possessing a sharp tongue and fierce claws, and terrifying with the sound of its bells.
With her mouth wide open, she was exceedingly dark blue and stained with the blood of enemies;
encircled by a garland of entrails, lion-faced, and terrible to behold, she possessed great thighs that reached far and could split apart the king of mountains. 33.
To be impelled by both arms, she is the bestower of victory in battle.
Tossing upward, whirling, leaping, bending, releasing, and piercing— these six paths are dependent upon the Śakti.
The *drughaṇa* should be made of iron, with a curved neck and a large head;
it should be fifty finger-breadths in height, and its circumference should be equal to a fist. Its functions are raising, falling, striking, and splitting. (36)
These four [forms] are indeed based on the *drughaṇa* posture and are characterized by a leaping motion.
The *tomara* has a wooden body with a metal head, is adorned with beautiful clusters of flowers, stands three cubits high, is red in color, and is straight. 37–38.
Raising up, withdrawing, and piercing— those kings who know the true nature of weapons call this triad "the gallop" (valgita).
The *nalikā* has a straight body, slender limbs, and a hollow in the middle.
The blue [flame], which severs the vital points (*marmacheda*), was drawn from the bow and arrows of Droṇa’s son.

Having understood that those three movements—seizing (*grahaṇa*), inflaming (*dhyāpana*), and stitching (*syūta*)—are dependent upon it, one shall conquer the enemies who have approached in battle. (40–41)

The *laguḍa* (club) should have slender legs, broad shoulders, and a thick head; its tip should be bound with iron, its body short and very stout, its frame firm, and it should be two cubits in height. 42.
Its body should be like that of a boar, its limbs strong, and likewise it should be elevated by two cubits.

Rising up, falling down, trampling, and likewise crushing—these are its four movements; a fifth does not exist here. With such a firm-bodied infantry unit, one should fight against the enemies. 43–44.
The noose has extremely subtle components, consists of iron ore, is triangular in shape, measures one span in circumference, and is adorned with lead beads;
its three functions are extension, coiling, and cutting. 45.
In this world, yogas are dependent on nooses, and nooses are dependent on the base.
But the wheel is circular in shape, provided with its own spokes at the end;
it is the color of indigo water, a mandala measuring two spans.
Twisting, whirling, hurling, cutting around, and crushing—
these are the five movements performed by the discus. Furthermore,
there is one named Dantakaṇṭaka, whose body is composed of iron spikes.
Broad at the front with a slender tail, its form resembling charcoal;
with upraised arms, a handle-like body, and fierce eyes—such is the *daṇḍaka*.
For the *dantakaṇṭaka*, there are two modes of movement: falling and piercing. (49–50)
Bṛsuṇḍī, however, has a large knot, a massive body, and an excellent hilt; she stands three arm-lengths high and possesses the fierce color of a black serpent.
Her two modes of movement are known as *yāpana* (advancing) and *ghūrṇana* (whirling). Thus she is endowed with these two gaits. 51.

"These are indeed declared to be 'liberated' (mukta); now hear concerning those that are not liberated. Thus ends the fourth chapter, titled "The Description of Liberated Weapons," in the illustrious *Nītiśāstra*, in the *Nītiprakāśikā*.
Chapter Five.

I shall describe to you that first unshakable vajra; listen to it. That vajra possesses immeasurable power and can assume any form at will; it was produced from the back-bone of Dadhīci and is the pacifier of all fiery splendors.
For the purpose of striking down the Asura Vṛtra, [the weapon] was augmented by the splendor of the gods;
it resembled ten million suns, was like the fire of universal destruction,
and possessed fangs a yojana in height and an exceedingly terrible tongue.
Resembling the Night of Doom (Kālarātri), it was covered with a hundred joints, five yojanas in width, ten yojanas in height,
encircled by a circle of swords, and possessed sharp points all around.
White as lightning and adorned with a broad handle,
the thunderbolt indeed always relies upon four movements: tossing, shaking, cutting, and likewise cleaving, along with the four brandishings.
The *īlī* is two cubits in height, with a hilt devoid of a pommel, dark in color, with a curved tip and a blade, and well-expanded at the five fingers;
it is used for the *saṃpāta*, the *samudīrṇa*, as well as for seizing and restraining. 7.
These four movements (valgitas) are indeed based on the *ilīma* [stance].
The *paraśu* [movement] has a slender staff-like form, a wide mouth, and faces forward;
its tip is like a half-moon, its body is dark, and its face is quivering. 9.

The handle of the axe has a peak-shaped form raised to the height of an arm; "felling" and "cutting" are the two qualities inherent in the axe. Gośīrṣa is like the head of a cow, with its two feet extended.
At its base it is provided with wooden mechanisms, and at the top it is adorned with an iron plate;
it is blue and red in color, three-edged,
with an excellent handle, sixteen finger-breadths in height, sharp-pointed, and broad in the middle.
Having honored it, Mahendra gave this ocean-seal to Manu;
for in the world, the *gośīrṣa* seal is indicative of sovereignty among kings. (13) Seizing by the fist, encircling, surrounding, and cutting down.
These four are declared to be the movements performed on the *gośīrṣa* [drum].
14. That which is called the *asidhenus* is measured by the height of the raised hand;
it is dark-colored, provided with a pommel and a hilt, and rests upon its three edges. 15.
Indeed, that which is two finger-breadths wide and serves to slay nearby enemies is called a *mekhalāgrathinī*; it is also known as a *khaḍgaputrikā*.
Furthermore, there are those for grasping by the fist-tip, as well as for splitting and piercing.

This [sacrificial ladle], possessing three wavy curves, should always be worn by the best of kings. The fire-stirring ladle (lavitra) should have a fierce body; it should be heavy at the back and sharp at the front, dark in color, five fingers wide, and one and a half cubits in height.
Bound with a heavy handle, it is the destroyer of buffaloes and other beasts;
its two arms are considered to be the exertion and the hurling of the sickle as it leaps.
Āstara is the knotted foot, possessing a long crest and large hands.
With bent hands, belly, and head, dark in complexion, and possessing two hands;
having mastered whirling, pulling, tearing, and the triple-leap, one should slay enemies in battle, supported by cavalry and infantry. 20–21.
The *kuṃta* (spear) should have a metallic shaft, sharp points, and six edges;
it is five cubits in height, with rounded feet, and is terrifying to behold.
[Its movements are] flying upward (*uḍḍhīna*), flying downward (*avaḍīna*), swooping down (*niḍīna*), and lurking on the ground (*bhūmilīnaka*).

The six paths (ṣaṇmārgāḥ) are based upon the spear (kunta): the horizontal (tiryaglīna), the buried (nikhāta), the one with a red body (raktadeha), the one with firm joints near [the base] (samīpadṛḍhaparvaka), the one of male proportions (puṃpramāṇa), and the straight (ṛju). In that [spear], there are two: whirling (bhramaṇa) and striking down (pātana). 23–24.
The *prāsa* (javelin), however, should be seven cubits in height and made of bamboo;
it has a metal head, sharp points, and is adorned with silk tassels.
There are also the *ākarṣa*, the *vikarṣa*, the *dhūnana*, and likewise the *vedhana*.
These four [deities] are based upon the Raktaprāsa. The Pināka, however, has three heads, a white tip, and cruel eyes;
it has a body of bell-metal, a head of iron, and measures four cubits in height.
His body and neck were adorned with a garland of bear-hair tassels and a circle of leather;
his trident possessed two functions, shaking and piercing, which corresponded to the two states of existence.
His mace was made of steel, with a hundred spokes and a broad head.
Terrible, with a covering of spikes and four arms raised high, her body as large as a chariot axle, her head adorned with a diadem,
protected by a golden girdle, she was the destroyer of elephants and mountains. 29–30.
Various mandalas, advances and retreats, diverse weapon-machines, and many different positions; the release from blows, avoidance, and circling about— 31.
Rushing forward, leaping, standing firm with the body poised, turning back,
retreating, springing down, springing up, the rightward circle, and likewise the leftward circle— 32–33.

The twenty paths of the mace (gadā) are: the thrown (āviddha), the cast aside (praviddha), the bursting (sphoṭana), the flaming (jvālana), the placed forward (upanyasta), the placed back (apanyasta), the mallet (mudgara), the subtle-footed (sūkṣmapāda), the headless (hīnaśīrṣa), and the three-handed (trihastavat). 34.
It is honey-colored, broad-shouldered, and weighs eight bhāras;
it has an excellent hilt, is circular, blue, and measured by the circumference of a hand.
Two types of action—whirling and striking—are employed with the mallet (mudgara). 35–36.
Sira was double-faced, Viśikha had iron feet and a mouth, Kṛṣan was the size of a man with a glossy complexion and the power to pull himself along or cast himself down;
Musala was devoid of eyes, a head, hands, and feet. 37.
At its base and tip there is an extreme connection; it consists of two parts, namely *pātana* and *pothana*.
The *paṭṭiśa* is of male proportions, having two edges and sharp points.
Its hilt is joined with hand-guards and is like a brother to the sword (*khaḍga*). 38–39.
The *mauṣṭika* [staff] should be known as having a fine handle, adorned with a height of one span (*prādeśa*),
with a sharp tip, a raised neck, and likewise a broad, dark belly (40).
There are various circular patterns and diverse positions.
Variegated movements like those of a cow urinating, as well as going forward and returning (gatapratyāgata), moving transversely, and likewise moving in curves;
the evading of blows, avoiding them, and running around. 41–42.
Rushing forward, leaping across, standing below, with form,
turning away, turning back, fleeing,
pursued, placed near, placed apart, arrived, and likewise the brandishing [of weapons]. 43.
O best of kings, these are said to be the *valgita* movements in the *mauṣṭika* style.
The *parigha* is circular in shape, the size of a palm tree, and easy to cross; its impact is achieved solely through strength—thus it should be understood by the wise. 44–45.
The staff should be made of bamboo, held in the fist, raised by the man, covered with small bells, variegated, and accompanied by crystal beads.
[It performs] striking, warding off, destroying, and liberation. 46.
These five, beginning with *abhidravaṇa*, are dependent upon the *mayūkhī*.
The *śataghnī* is provided with spikes, made of solid black iron, resembling a mallet, four cubits long, circular, and equipped with a handle. 47–48.
"This [movement] of the mace, as it brandishes, has been described by me to you as 'mayā' (by me),
O best of kings; these twenty are called 'amuktāyudha' (unreleased weapons),
and the settled conclusion is that there are thirty-two when including those designated by the term 'muktāmukta' (released-unreleased)."
The sword fashioned by Brahmā has been described to you separately (verse 50).
O King, these undergo transformation according to the succession of the Yugas,
as well as in accordance with the firmness of the body and the succession of the Yugas, O King.
According to the strength of the body and likewise according to the capacity of the intellect,
there are machines made of iron and lead that discharge pellets, as well as stone-engines and other artificial contrivances. 51–52.
O King, in the Kali age, these will become aids for treacherous warfare:
heated oil, resin of the *sarja* tree, molasses, iron slag, and fierce sand;
honey, jars of venomous snakes, sharp-edged spears, and massive boulders. (53)
Saws, smoke-bombs, chaff, charcoal, and the like—
these, O protector of the earth, will increasingly become the instruments of those who, through the growth of unrighteousness, long for deceitful warfare.
The Hūṇas, Pulindas, Śabaras, Barbaras, Paplavas, Śakas, Mālavas, Kauṅkaṇas, Āndhras, Colas, Pāṇḍyas, and Keralas;
as well as other Mlecchas, those born of cows, Caṇḍālas, Śvapacas, and the wicked.

The Māvellakas, Lalitthas, Kirātas, and Kukkuṛas—these are indeed sinful and of mixed birth; how shall they know the Dharma? In this lowest age, they will be devoted to the fault of social confusion (saṃkara).
Thus, O child, these duties have been declared by me to you, who desire the welfare of the world and are intent on listening. What more shall I tell you?
Thus ends the fifth chapter, titled "The Description of Amuktāyudha," in the illustrious *Nītiśāstra*, the *Nītiprakāśikā*.
The Sixth Chapter.
Now I shall describe the battle arrays (*vyūha*) which crush the enemy army, for the purpose of confounding the enemy and for the sake of arranging the components of the force. 1.
Having ascertained the increase of his own strength and the calamities of the enemy,

he should march against the foe after deploying his army with three times the enemy's forces. [The formations are] the staff (daṇḍa), the snake (bhoga), the detached (asaṃhata), and the circle (maṇḍala) array.
These are the four primary battle arrays; of these, I shall now declare the variations:
Pradara, Dṛḍhaka, Satya, Cāpa, Bhūsvara, Akṣi, Supratiṣṭha, Apratiṣṭha, Śyena, Vijaya, and Sañjaya.
Viśāla, Vijaya, Sūcī, Sthūṇa, Akarṇa, Camūmukha, Sukhāsya, and Vijaya— thus the staff (daṇḍa) consists of seventeen parts.
Furthermore, there are the Gomūtrikā, the Haṃsikā, the Saṃcārī, and likewise the Śakaṭa.
Thus, "they fall like saws" refers indeed to the five types of fissures in the coils:
the half-moon, the tortoise-shell, the thunderbolt, the crab, and likewise the horn; the crow's foot and the lizard are also recorded as others.
Those skilled in military arrays say that the uncombined array is of six kinds:
Sarvabhadra, Durjaya, and Maṇḍala, which is also of two kinds;
as well as Vārāhī, Makara-vyūha, Gāruḍa, and Krauñca.
Padma and the others are recorded as distinct from these because of a deficiency in their limbs;
O King, it should be understood by the wise that there are thousands of such arrays (vyūhas) among Rākṣasas, gods, and humans, fashioned by the diversity of their intellects. 9–10.
The chest, the two flanks, the wings, the center, the back, the reserve, and the two tips— by those learned in the science of military arrays, this is called the seven-limbed array (saptāṅga-vyūha).
O King, elephants should be placed in the front, chariots in the rear, and horses on both flanks.
Keeping the foot-soldiers in the rear of the formation, one shall be victorious. According to the requirements of each specific task, one should deploy chariots, elephants, horses,
men, cavalry, chariots, elephants, infantry, and cavalry, as well as chariots.
Having harnessed them in due order and having carefully considered the place and time, he should send forth the elephants at the front, accompanied by their retinues;
thus the best of kings, prepared for the expedition, sets out together with his entire army.
Then, having seen [the enemy], he should set out and employ his forces in an advance;
desiring an assault, he should then carry out a frontal attack.
He should employ those who are capable of seizing [the enemy], those from the Kaukṣika region, those who are swift-footed, and those who are eager for the fray.
One should station vigorous and battle-hardened elephants in the midst of the army.
Young elephants, calves, and small ones, as well as those used for riding, should be kept in training;
and even the small elephants, when they have become fierce with rut, should be made fit for harnessing.
He should also inspect the elephant corps, as well as those traveling on the main roads;
furthermore, he should visit those outside the inner apartments, the neighbors along the back streets,
the inhabitants of the suburban towns, and the merchants of the capital city.
He saw eunuchs, dwarfs, the elderly, children, and the sick;
those with wounds and those without eyes; the lame, the deformed, and the very weak;
as well as flower-carts and thrones provided with cushions.
And likewise those who follow the process of production, as well as the implements of war;
the granaries, armories, and machine-sheds;
the mountainous storehouses for grain, and whatever else is emaciated or weak. (21–22)
The lord of men should cause the warriors to dwell within his own domain for the purpose of crushing the enemy, and he should duly provide protection for them with brave men;
likewise, he should station those who are powerful and swift-footed against the approaching foe.
He should dispatch ahead scouts, messengers, spies, and warriors skilled in combat;
likewise, he should send his own highly exalted elephant, bearing the banners and flags of victory, at the head of the army along with his swift forces.
He likewise [inquired after] those who go before, those who follow behind, as well as those who assist, those who move alongside, the scouts, the couriers, the staff-bearers, the followers,
those bearing swords and shields, and the panegyrists and bards.
For the sake of his own protection, the king should station his own cavalry in the front;
he should station swift, well-bred horses fit for the back and for the chariot, as well as sturdy horses equipped with armor, in the rear and in close proximity to him.
One should construct for the month of Āśvina a large wooden structure with a peak, complete with a moat, containing wealth, grain, and weapons;
it should be equipped with archers, water, husks, charcoal, and artisans. 29.

While fighting with his enemies, the best of kings should rely upon [allies] who have many resources and are trustworthy; having secured internal family members, the king should employ wise men as primary remedies to carry out the requital of enmity. (30–31)
Having established the primary reception of tribute and arranged for the subsequent collection,

that best of kings protected his own kingdom and the guilds of his citizens, while providing gifts to those who sought refuge; having stationed his soldiers and the guards at the borders, he remained vigilant.
He should dispatch many road-makers ahead of him— artisans,
laborers, staff-bearers, diggers, carpenters, as well as surveyors, planters, and bridge-builders. (33–34)

Likewise, having dispatched those who are experts in the knowledge of terrain, skilled hunters, and conversant with forests— those who are highly learned and capable of discerning an enemy force situated in difficult terrain— he should lead his army after having arranged for its protection.
Avoiding cremation grounds, temples,
hermitages of great seers, sacred fords, and shrines, one should not stand upon husks, charcoal, ashes, hair, or potsherds. (36–37)
In a region that is sweet, not saline, auspicious, meritorious, and surrounded by water,
the king should cause his camp to be established for the prosperity of his own army;
he should likewise disperse the enemy's outposts as well as those who move about alone and are harmful.
He should march around the army, surrounded by warriors,
personally inspecting the vulnerable points of the enemy kings and deploying his forces on all sides to thwart the enemy's preparations. (39–40)
Having issued instructions for the defensive works and dispatched spies, he assigned costly camps, each distinct from the others, for his own warriors—
camps well-supplied with water and wood and most difficult to assail.

Having provided food and drink, and being endowed with wealth and grain, he engaged hundreds of wise and skilled artisans who were paid wages, as well as highly proficient physicians equipped with all necessary instruments. (42–43)
Having set aside abundant wealth for the warriors, as well as garments and ornaments to be given to them, he should fight the enemies without hesitation.
He should provide mounts for those whose mounts and warriors have been lost.
In battle, the lord of the earth should cause weapons to be given to those who are unarmed; likewise, he should provide saddle-cloths,
bits, housings, and other trappings, as well as fans, head-ornaments, armor, and elephant-blankets.
Bowstrings, bows, armor, weapons, many quivers, great engines, iron arrows, javelins, and battle-axes;
ropes, stakes, pegs for the feet, and iron fetters for the legs. 47.
Axes, hatchets, adzes, and even knives; wheels, iron bands, saws, and leather bags; baskets, spades, needles, and those suitable for sewing. 48–49.
He gave him long-eared oxen, mules, and camels capable of traveling great distances;
medicines for elephants, horses, and men;
various musical instruments; and likewise the honey of the Kirātas.
And also cotton mattresses from the silk-cotton tree, as well as those made of stone and joined with iron;
and wretched mats made of wood, and vessels of iron and copper,
and brass, and hammers, and whetstones, and axes as well.
Here too were wagon wheels, sandals, thigh-protectors, whips,
*viśvakadrū* birds, bamboos, snares, hooks, water-basins,
scented oils, and whatever else such as yellow dyes.
He should properly arrange those preparations for the army's departure.
He should appoint chariot-warriors among the soldiers who are experts in riding horses;
likewise, he should appoint those well-trained in chariots as horsemen.
The king should appoint both of them as skilled warriors mounted on the backs of elephants;

indeed, he should also appoint such men as foot-soldiers, as well as for the role of charioteers, for positions on the necks of elephants, and as experts in protecting the wheels [of the chariot]. 56.
Or in other cases of violent crimes, the king should appoint skilled men for those tasks.
(57) Regarding the thirty-two strategic elements of warfare that exist here according to political science, he should ensure that his entire fourfold army is well-established within them. (58)
Advancing ahead of the march, entering forest strongholds, opening up unmade paths and maintaining those already made (59),
dispelling fears, and likewise the breaking down of ramparts.
The treasury policy consists of protection from fear and the reconciliation of those who have been divided.
Furthermore, they declare that the duties of elephants in a fort include carrying heavy loads, breaking down trees, and obstructing the enemy's horses. (60–61)
Leading the second army, protecting the elephants, repairing broken ranks, repelling the enemy from a distance,
obstructing the enemies, and maintaining a position at the gate of the formation. 62.

The ritual of the great roar—these they declare to be the craft of charioteering (rathakarma). Furthermore, knowledge of forests, directions, and roads; the protection of supplies and reinforcements; the clearing of paths; and terrifying the enemy by the sound of neighing.
Following up, retreating, the swift accomplishment of tasks,
and plundering— these are declared to be the duties of the cavalry against enemy forces. (65) Furthermore, there is the clearing of wells, watering places, roads, and the camp.
The establishment of the camp, the execution of forced labor,
the protection of the treasury, the armory, and the granary, as well as the construction of fortifications and walls, are declared to be the duties of the infantry.

A ground for infantry that is free of trees, large stones, shrubs, anthills, and thorns; which is clear of obstacles and not excessively uneven, is considered suitable. It should likewise be free of mud, devoid of stakes, and cleared of rocks. (68)
The ground for horses is considered level, with soil capable of enduring the impact of their hooves.
The chariot-ground is proclaimed to be free of furrows and pits, devoid of trees and shrubs, firm enough to withstand the pressure of wheels, and pleasant.

The excellent tree to be crushed is a creeper; it is free from mud, without chasms, accessible, yet its mountain-like terrain is uneven. The commander of the entire army should be a man of noble birth who has conquered his senses.
He is one who has witnessed past calamities, is skillful, handsome, and a favorite of the king; he is a courtier who understands gestures and is expert in the conduct of armies;
he is bold and a consoler of his own warriors on the field of battle.

The commanders of the *akṣauhiṇīs* should likewise be appointed separately; they too, being protected by him, should remain under the control of the general. [This applies] to the foot-soldier, the vanguard of the army, the *gulma*, and the *gaṇa*. 74.

Separate commanders should indeed be appointed for the *vāhinī*, the *pṛtanā*, and the *camū*; likewise, those established in the training of warriors should be made leaders of the *anīkinī*. Furthermore, lords of two or three [units] should be appointed according to the requirements of the task.
Day by day, the commanders of the army, and not the soldiers nor other people, should issue distinct orders according to their own strength;
they should move about marked with their own insignia for the purpose of circulating their commands. (77)

They declare that defensive operations are for the purpose of destroying enemies. (78) Whosoever was previously appointed to the command of the army shall remain fixed in his senior status; those who follow him are under his authority. (79)
Having appointed the commanders of the eight akṣauhiṇīs as lords of the divisions starting with the Pācya, and having bound all the soldiers according to their seniority,
[the king] dismissed them after they had been restrained by the king and had given their assent to his command.

One should slay the night-stalkers in the army who oppose the king’s command. Three well-trained commanders should be appointed for the opposing force— superior, inferior, and middling— who remain obedient to the orders of the senior leader.
Day after day, one should cause the army to change its positions and urge it forward;
for an army well-stationed in one place may even cause suspicion of oneself. That minister who is loyal and capable of bearing the burden of the king's affairs [should be appointed].
The king himself should rely upon the command of that Sainyapāla;
when his own army is rallied, he should have the enemies fought by the *saṃśapta* warriors, while the king himself, desiring victory, should remain at the *vīrāśaṃsana* station. 84–85.
When his own army is fleeing in all directions, he himself, having equipped his forces with iron armor, should personally go to the rear and conquer the enemies;
this is the battle array formed by a large army at a distance of two *gavyūtis*.
That army is called "shaven-headed" (muṇḍānīka) when it consists of heroes who lack umbrellas and chowries.
When a fresh deed has been accomplished, the king, showing honor and boasting of his success, should especially bestow the *pūrṇapātra* upon the warriors. 87–88.
One should joyfully give a million cows to the slayer of a king;
half of that for the slaying of his son, and likewise for the slaying of a commander-in-chief.
For the slaying of a commander of an *akṣauhiṇī* army, they declare half of that [amount] to be given.
For the killing of a minister or a counselor, one should cause half of that [fine] to be paid.
An anīkinī, a camū, a pṛtanā, a vāhinī, a gaṇa, a gulma, a senāmukha, and a patti—[for the killing] of these, [the fine is as follows]. For one who slays their leader, [the fine is as stated]. 90–91.

One should cause them to pay half of those respective amounts by gradually reducing it by one-half; furthermore, having received more than their wages, they might commit acts of violence (sāhasa) against the commander of an akṣauhiṇī, or his second-in-command, or his third-in-command. 92.
Likewise, from the lord of two *camūs* up to the lord of armies (*pṛtanā*), as far as the commander of a *anīkinī*, one receives rewards from the king;
in this same manner, even further on, honor should be bestowed upon the commanders. 93–94.
The king, having captured one who has fled while still armed and handed him over to his own soldier,
should indeed honor that soldier and grant him five cows. However, [he should not reward] one who has fled, who was being paid wages, who is unarmed, and who desires to save his life.
Having seized them, the king should present them to the one who brings the news, and he should give three *varvas* to the messengers.
Having cut off the head of an elephant, an elephant-riders, or a great chariot-warrior, and having presented it to the king, he deserves two thousand [pieces of gold]. (96–97)
Having slain a preeminent horseman or likewise a commander of infantry, one becomes worthy of a thousand cows from the king;
and he who captures an elephant or a chariot from the enemy army [is likewise worthy]. 98.
Let him receive an honor of fifty years' salary from the king in this world; at every stage of the journey, food must be provided for his servants,
for while they remain on the road, this provision— exceeding their wages— is due to the recognition of their fatigue.
In other cases of violent crimes, the king should indeed grant rewards exceeding their wages for the sake of maintaining order in the world;
he should also give garments to the soldiers and wages to the washermen.

Medicines for the sick should be provided by that very same wage [of the soldiers]. (102) As for wealth acquired from a foreign kingdom, the king, having divided it into two halves, should give one half to the warriors and take the other half for himself. (103)

A soldier who seizes a horse or even a well-equipped wagon shall receive a quarter of its value as a reward, honored by the king; likewise for those who recover weapons that have been discarded or plundered by enemies in battle. (104)
The king should provide wages to his own soldiers, even after deducting [expenses].
To those who have died in battle for his sake at the hands of enemies, and to those who have been supported by him through service, their livelihood must be provided. 105–106.

For those who have died and even for those who are still living— his own followers who were formerly devoted to service— their former half-portion of sustenance shall continue; furthermore, the young warriors who fell facing the enemy in battle did not die [in vain].
For those who are incapable of serving kings, the first half of their livelihood [is prescribed].
For one who strikes at the vital points (marmas) of an enemy for the purpose of harming him, the fee for that action is proclaimed to be double. 108–109.
One should employ those who shatter enemy armies, who are intent on scaling fortresses,
and who increase their own kingdom with heaps of wealth. Having thus appointed the warriors according to these qualifications, [one should proceed].
But the king, having accomplished his purpose by slaying his enemies,
attains great fame and prosperity, and, being honored by the best of kings, he is glorified. 111
Thus ends the sixth chapter, titled "The Discourse on the Leadership of the Army," in the illustrious *Nītiśāstra*, in the *Nītiprakāśikā*.
Now begins the seventh chapter:
"I shall now explain the army for the purpose of augmenting the leadership of the forces."

O Lord of the Earth, may it be well with you; I shall enumerate for you, starting from a single *patti* up to an *akṣauhiṇī*, the number of chariots, elephants, horses, and especially the foot soldiers stationed in the army. 1-2.
A *patti* forms the face of an army; from it comes a *senāmukha*, then a *gulma*, a *gaṇa*, a *vāhinī*, a *pṛtanā*, a *camū*, a *anīkinī*, and finally an *akṣauhiṇī* is recorded.
These are indeed the specific divisions of an army; now I shall tell you about the principal foot-soldiers (*pattis*).
Chariots, elephants, horses, and especially foot soldiers—[one chariot, one elephant, five men, and three horses] constitute what is called a *patti*; I shall now describe their auxiliaries. 4–5.
Ten elephants belong to this chariot; one hundred horses with their attendants, and a thousand men are said to be the retinue by the king's command.
For each single elephant, there are one hundred horses that march along.
There are one thousand foot-soldiers as followers for each of the front-limbs [of the chariot];
and for each single horse, there are one thousand foot-soldiers.
Having joined these ten leaders together, this is the complete enumeration.

One chariot, ten elephants, a thousand horses, and a hundred thousand foot soldiers constitute an *anīka*; the same calculation applies to the subsequent units as well. Each successive unit is named after its constituent parts, which increase threefold in each case.
The wise say that ten times an *anīkinī* is an *akṣauhiṇī*.
At the front of the army, there are three times as many chariots and elephants;
indeed, there are thirty thousand foot-soldiers and three thousand horses.
In the Gulma formation, nine chariots are prescribed; they know there to be ninety elephants, nine thousand horses, and nine hundred thousand foot soldiers.
In the formation called Gaṇa, however, there are twenty-seven excellent śatāṅgas.
The noble ones say there are two hundred and seventy elephants;
twenty-seven thousand gandharvas are proclaimed, and twenty-seven lakhs of foot soldiers are recorded here. 13–14.
In that army, chariots are said to have been deployed, numbering eight hundred and ten;
likewise, lotus-seated elephants (padminas) are proclaimed here to be one thousand and eighty-one.
Furthermore, horses are declared to number eighty-one thousand.
Indeed, eighty-one lakhs of them were renowned as foot-soldiers;
there were two hundred and forty-three chariots for the army,
and two thousand, three hundred and thirty elephants.
O Indra among kings, there were exactly forty-three thousand horses, two hundred thousand, and twenty million men;
and as for the foot soldiers, learn from me that there were four million three hundred thousand.
I shall describe in detail the enumeration within the seventh array known as the *camū*.
In this *camū*, seven hundred and twenty-nine chariots are recorded, as well as seven thousand two hundred and ninety [infantry]. 19–20.
There were seven hundred thousand and twenty-nine thousand elephants; now hear the number of horses and foot soldiers, O King:
seven crores and twenty-nine lakhs.
Those who know the principles of calculation and subsist by their intellect uttered the count:
"O sinless one, I shall now tell you the calculation of two thousand one hundred and eighty-seven chariots and as many elephants in an *anīkinī*. (22-23)
O King, listen with a concentrated mind to the number of horses: twenty-one thousand, eight hundred, and seventy.
Furthermore, there are two million one hundred and eighty-seven thousand.
O lord of men, know that there are twenty-one crores of foot soldiers;
O best among the wise, know that there are eighty-seven lakhs [of horses];
and ten times this would constitute an akṣauhiṇī—listen now to that description.
O lord of men, they know that in an akṣauhiṇī there are twenty-one thousand, eight hundred, and seventy chariot-riders;
and two hundred thousand and eighteen thousand foot soldiers, O lord of men. (27)
Likewise, there were seven hundred elephants; this is the count. O Lord of the Earth, there were two crores, eighteen lakhs, and seventy thousand Gandharvas who move with great speed.

Two arbudas, eighteen koṭis, and seventy lakhs of foot soldiers— this much is said to constitute an akṣauhiṇī; [yet] these chariots and elephants [belong] to the king, apart from the arrangement of the akṣauhiṇīs.

Other horses are independent, serving as the king's rear-guards. Today, the banners and cloths should be displayed on the limbs [of the chariots] separately and with particular care, in order to distinguish one's own army from that of the enemy. 31-32.
The salary for the crown prince shall be five thousand *varvāṇas*,
and for the commander of the entire army, four thousand;
that same salary shall also be given to an *atiratha*, and three thousand *varvāṇas* to a [standard] *ratha*.
The king should grant two thousand [paṇas] as the monthly salary for a mahāratha;
furthermore, one thousand for a chariot-warrior, half that for an elephant-warrior, and five hundred as the salary for an ardharatha. (34–35)
To one such chariot-warrior and likewise to an elephant-rider,
he should give three hundred *niṣkas*, for they are the heads of their respective families (36). And that commander of all the king's cavalry deserves three thousand.
The commander of the infantry is also the recipient of a two-thousand [coin] salary;
the leader of a thousand infantrymen is recorded as receiving five hundred,
and likewise, for the lord of a thousand horses, the wage shall be one thousand.
The wage for a foot soldier shall be five gold pieces;
for the commander of a hundred, seven; for one who rides a horse, [eight]; and for the elephant driver, the charioteer, the standard-bearer, and the wielder of the discus, [the same]. 39.
To the lord of three hundred foot-soldiers, to the one who moves with travelers and camels;
likewise to the sovereign of the Vārtikas, to the lord of the staff-bearers, to the lord of the charioteers, bards, and panegyrists, and to the master of provisions.
To the one who provides the wages for the army and to those intent on counting the soldiers,
the monthly salary shall be fifteen *varvāṇas*; furthermore,
according to their respective duties and by rotation among the families.
The wages for the soldiers, however, should be determined according to the specific requirements of each time.
In battles, brave kings who, desiring to slay one another, fight with their utmost strength and do not turn their backs, go to heaven. 43–44.
While fighting his enemies in battle, he should not strike them with deceptive weapons, nor with poisoned, flaming, or barbed missiles, nor with various kinds of mechanical traps.
He should not kill one who has climbed a tree, nor a eunuch, nor one who joins his palms in supplication.
One should not strike one with disheveled hair, nor one who is seated, nor one who says "I am yours";
nor one who is fast asleep, nor one who is bowing down, nor one who is naked, nor one who is unarmed,
nor one who is looking on while engaged in combat, nor one who has encountered another foe.

One should not strike one who has met with the calamity of weapons, nor one who is distressed, nor one who is severely wounded, nor one who is inferior, nor one who has turned away, nor one who has taken refuge in an anthill; 48.
nor should one kill one who holds grass in his mouth, nor a woman, nor one wearing the dress [of another].
One who causes such persons to be killed by soldiers would become a sinner.
Such a person, however, should take whatever evil karma was previously accumulated by the one being killed and give his own merit to them. 49–50.
In the auspicious month of Mārgaśīrṣa, or in Phālguna or Caitra, the lord of the earth should undertake a military expedition when he perceives certain victory; however,
while an enemy’s ally remains in power, he should remain most vigilant with secret efforts.
For he who returns after having gone away is indeed the most dangerous enemy.
One should lead the army in the Daṇḍa array, or the Śakaṭa, or the Varāha, the Garuḍa, the Sūcī, or the Makara array.

From whichever direction danger from an enemy may arise, one should extend the force there; the commander-in-chief and the army officers should station themselves in all directions. From whichever direction fear arises, the one who is afraid should designate that as the eastern direction.

One should engage those enemies in battle by deploying them in the *sūcī* (needle) and *vakra* (crooked) arrays. Furthermore, one should station reliable troops as outposts on all sides—men who are skilled in both holding their positions and fighting, who are fearless, and who slay the enemy. 55–56.
One should obstruct the enemy's fodder, food, water, and wealth, and personally observe the movements of the enemies as they fight;
one should instigate those who are susceptible to instigation and cause division among those who are disunited. 57.

A king should sustain greedy enemies' warriors with gifts as is appropriate; however, he should discipline his own such [subordinates] without hesitation. Devoted to the vital secrets of others, he should conceal his own methods. 58–59.
For when the time of battle has arrived, [there are] army commanders who neglect their own warriors who are intent on flight and opposed to their commands,
and who fight under false pretexts while being excessively greedy.
And for those who turn their backs on others, who cause mutual dissension among warriors,
who clearly proclaim their own paths to enemies under the guise of deception, who provide passage to foes, and who rejoice in the calamity of their own kin. (61–62)
The king who possesses discernment must inflict the death penalty upon them even for a very great offense; however, the execution of envoys is censured.
That king who releases those who should not be punished and causes those who deserve proper punishment to be slain [incurs sin].
By him who follows righteousness, it shall be as if a hundred sacrifices had been performed.
Thus ends the seventh chapter, titled "The Array of the Army," in the illustrious *Nītiśāstra*, the *Nītiprakāśikā*.
Chapter Eight.
I shall proclaim the duties of kings, how a monarch should conduct himself; for in this world, the eternal dharma of a king is precisely the pleasing of the people.
For when a pregnant woman, setting aside her own dear and mentally cherished [husband], [goes forth...]
Just as one provides nourishment for the benefit of the embryo, so should one act for the benefit of the subjects;
since he is fashioned from the portions of the eight world-protectors,
the king should therefore overcome all beings with his splendor.
He becomes Agni and Vāyu; he is Arka and Soma;
by his power, he is Kubera, Varuṇa, and Mahendra.
Even as a child, a lord of the earth must not be disregarded on the grounds that he is merely a human being.
For this is a great divinity who dwells in human form.
A single fire burns only the man who approaches it too closely;
but the king’s fire consumes the entire family, along with its cattle and its store of wealth.
In his favor dwells the goddess Padmā Śrī and victory in his prowess;
death resides in his anger; therefore, he is the refuge of all. Those dwelling in his cities and kingdoms have their wealth unhidden.
The king who knows what to adopt and what to reject should act in this manner: rising in the latter part of the night, he should contemplate the determination of affairs,
having himself understood the merits and defects with a clear mind regarding what ought to be done.
Having meditated firmly upon the Divine with the heart and having had the recitation of auspicious texts performed,

one should become pure and perform the ritual of grasping the auspicious object according to the rules. Then, having completed the daily rites and having made the daily offerings, [one should proceed].
Having bowed to those who are advanced in the three Vedas, one should abide by their instruction;
for with a disciplined soul, one should always learn self-restraint from them. Indeed, even forest-dwellers have attained kingdoms through discipline.
One should apply oneself day and night to the conquest of the senses;
for this world is always under the control of one who has conquered his senses.
Free from the group of six internal enemies, devoted to the Vedas and scriptures, and pure—
When the morning has passed, the king, adorned with ornaments, should proceed to the assembly hall; seated upon a high throne, he should deliberate on the administration of the kingdom,
having seated upon the seat of justice a wise Brahmin who serves as his domestic priest.
One who merely lives by his birth may, at will, be called a "pseudo-Brāhmaṇa" (brāhmaṇabruva) and serve as the king's expounder of dharma; but a Śūdra shall never under any circumstances do so.
For that king for whom a Śūdra performs the discernment of dharma—
That kingdom of his perishes while he looks on, like a cow sinking in the mud.
He should appoint seven or eight ministers who are hereditary, learned in the scriptures, brave, skilled in hitting the mark, of noble birth, and thorough examiners.

A king devoted to his interests should appoint two or three good ministers who speak according to justice; together with them, he should deliberate on affairs in the capital city. Furthermore, he should appoint gatekeepers, bodyguards, leaders of the assembly, and messengers.
Having issued the command according to the prescribed rule, he should remain attentive in mind.
He should appoint a messenger who is learned in all the scriptures, one who understands gestures, facial expressions, and physical movements, who is pure, observant, and well-wishing.

In accordance with the Dharmaśāstras, the king, together with his ministers and his domestic priest, should examine legal cases along with learned Brāhmaṇas. Having supervised the military operations and having fixed their wages, [he should provide for them].

Having properly considered the livelihood of the wretched, the blind, and the miserable, and having understood their income and expenditure as well as their future prosperity, he then ensured the security,
welfare, and sustenance of the farmers.
Having learned from indirect reports that they are afflicted by the calamity of famine,
he should give his own wealth to them as is appropriate, and having strengthened them,
he should with a composed mind recover his property from them once they are well-nourished. 25.
Having had a document of the deadline written by his own hand and delivered to them,
and having released the petty officials from fear, the king himself bestowed garments as rewards upon them according to the prescribed rite.
Having intimidated them with his words, the king— whose heart was moist with compassion and who was skilled in the arts of conciliation and bribery—
established regulations for them after investigating the conduct of the officials through his spies.
The promoter of the science of punishment should administer instruction to the wicked.
Where the dark-complexioned, red-eyed Punishment stalks, destroying sin, there the subjects do not go astray, provided that the leader perceives rightly. (29–30)
Those who engage in buying and selling at improper times, those who act out of self-interest, those who impose taxes upon the subjects, those who obstruct the duties of their masters,
and those who cause terror among the people— these shall be punished with severe penalties and suffering.
[The punishment applies] to those who, out of the fault of greed, steal the property of gods, Brahmins, or their own kin;

to those who obstruct the king’s commands; to those whose minds are intent on treason against the king; and to those who recount the deeds of their own king while [he is] in the presence of a hostile king.

For those who breach embankments, those who release prisoners, those who are negligent regarding royal property, those who embezzle from the royal treasury, and those who, while holding official positions, take half of their wages; 34. [the king shall confiscate their entire property].
For those who cause dissension within their own faction, whose minds are devoted to malevolent magic (abhicāra),
who are intent on denial in the presence of the king regarding their own words,
who treat the king's property as something else, and who destroy tanks and groves; 35–36.

For the purpose of training them, spies should be employed; having ascertained their transgressions from them in accordance with the truth, one should subsequently instruct them according to the path of political ethics (nīti), through the loss of office and confinement in prison. 37.
By means of shackles and fetters, as well as banishment from the kingdom;
by confiscation of all property and the commissioning of base tasks;
and by being clothed in a single garment or a coarse cloak while stationed at crossroads.
Through the authority of disciplinary rotations, by inflicting physical hardships,
by means of soft whips or lashes with a whip, and likewise by disfigurement—
by these and other such methods according to the scriptures, one should train those under his authority.
But having seen those who laugh at people instructed by the king,
the king should likewise instruct those who mock or revile him, as well as those who laugh at the king's wives;
and knowing those villagers standing on the road, the king should instruct them.
For a king who is always mild becomes weak in every respect, and the world is terrified of one who is harsh; therefore, he should practice both.
First, let the king acquire a kingdom, then a wife, and then wealth.
If there were no king in this world, from where would there be a wife, and from where wealth?
