(44) Servants who desire the welfare of the king should carry out their duties in accordance with his income; if they report otherwise, they shall partake of punishment. (45)
The king should appoint a lord of a village, likewise a lord of ten villages,
a lord of twenty, a lord of a hundred, and a lord of a thousand.
The village headman shall protect the villagers from the evils of the village.
The group of ten should report them to the leader of ten;
the leader of twenty should report all that has occurred to the people of the district, and he in turn should report everything to the protector of a hundred villages. 47–48.
Whatever food belongs to the village headman, that the headman enjoys; for he is traditionally considered a member of the kingdom by virtue of his share of gold and grain.
Therefore, the lord of ten must be supported by him, and likewise, the lord of twenty is so ordained.
The superintendent of a hundred villages deserves to enjoy one village with due honor;
the lord of a thousand villages, however, deserves a branch-city,
for he is a leader of hundreds of villages and is worthy of the seat of a world-protector.
Whatever village duties there may be, and whatever state business there may be, some minister who knows the Dharma should attend to them with vigilance.
And in every city, there should be one person who oversees all affairs.
High-ranking, of terrible appearance like a planet among the stars,
that successful man should constantly move about among them all; indeed, he should thoroughly calculate their livelihoods through his own spies throughout the kingdom.

O Yudhiṣṭhira, these subjects must be protected from those appointed to various offices of protection who are intent on killing, who desire evil, who seize the property of others, and who are deceitful; for the taxes and legal systems of former kings were of diverse kinds.
The lord of the earth should act in such a way that they do not decline.
A king should not take a toll from Brāhmaṇas, nor should he ever collect taxes from them; for a ruler of men should never be the master of a Brāhmaṇa’s wealth.

The king, acting for the benefit of his subjects, should personally ensure that income is made extensive and expenditure is made very slight; likewise, he should construct embankments, lakes, ponds, and his own dwellings. 58.
One who has established a good path should likewise protect rows of trees and groves;
he should show honor to the twice-born who are advanced in learning,
and by means of punishments such as public humiliation, he should compel those Brahmins who neglect their duties to apply themselves to sacred knowledge.
One should seek what has not been obtained through righteous means; what has been obtained, one should protect with effort;
what has been protected, one should constantly increase; and what has been increased, one should bestow upon worthy recipients (pātra). One should give enjoyments and various riches to the Brahmins.

This is an inexhaustible treasure for kings: the bestowing [of land] upon Brahmins. Having given land or having established a permanent endowment, the monarch should cause a deed to be drawn up for the information of future benevolent rulers. (62–63)
Having granted land and other gifts, the king should cause a righteous edict to be inscribed on a copper plate or a cloth, recording the location, lineage, and other details.
The merit of protecting what has been given by another is twice that of giving it oneself. (64)

By seizing what has been given by another, one's own gift shall become fruitless. A king should not subvert the established boundaries or the means of livelihood created by a former king; by destroying them, he becomes censured.
For counsel is always the root of victory for kings;
therefore, a king should deliberate on counsel together with his ministers.
Having ascended a mountain peak or having gone to a secluded palace, [he should do so].
The lord of the earth should deliberate in a forest or in a place free from obstacles (68).
He should deliberate with vigilance on the roof of a palace, in a forest, or in a place that is without pillars, without windows, and without any internal walls or coverings (69).
That king who, even if devoid of treasure, enjoys the earth for a long time because ordinary people do not come together to know his counsel;
[he likewise enjoys it] even over those who are dull-witted, blind, mute, deaf, one-eyed, intoxicated, or base.
At the time of deliberation on counsel, one should avoid women, barbarians, the diseased, and the deformed;
one should employ the four expedients, the six measures, and the three rising factors,
as well as the three powers and the successes, in consultation with one's ministers.
Conciliation, bribery, sowing dissension, and force— these fourfold means should be employed by those who live by their intellect in all undertakings.
Conciliation is to be known as fivefold, as well as compliance with others.
Mutual assistance, proclaiming their virtues, making known one's kinship, and offering oneself— knowing these five ways, both in brief and in detail, one becomes happy. (74-75)
They say that giving is fivefold: the surrendering of one's own wealth; the joy in accepting another's goods; the bestowing of a previously unowned object;
the incitement toward another's property; and the clearing of debts. (76)
When one’s own weakness is evident, the application of this [strategy] against the enemy’s side is the prescribed method (77).
Sowing dissension is threefold: first, winning over one of the two parties through affection; likewise, breaking the friendship between them; and finally, issuing a threat (78).
Punishment is proclaimed to have three varieties: the seizure of wealth, infliction of suffering, and physical chastisement.
An alliance (saṃdhi) should be understood as having two characteristics, being connected with both the present and the future.

War is declared to be of two kinds: that waged by a king for the sake of a specific objective, whether at the proper time or an improper time; and that waged against a treacherous ally. Furthermore, war may be undertaken alone when a task arises by chance that must be accomplished by oneself.
Marching in conjunction with an ally is said to be of two kinds:
[the army] being gradually depleted by fate or by past karma, and [the army] being dispatched out of deference to an ally; thus, the "march with a settled mind" is of two kinds. (81–82)

For the sake of achieving stability for both the army and the master, those who know its virtues and defects declare that duplicity (dvaidha) is of two kinds: when one has ascertained with certainty either one's own deficiency or one's superiority. (84)
Seeking refuge is of two kinds: for the purpose of alleviating financial distress, and for the purpose of obtaining the support of virtuous men when one is being oppressed by enemies.
(85) Rise is traditionally held to be threefold: decline, stability, and growth.

Power is considered to be threefold, consisting of the divisions of majesty (*prabhu*), counsel (*mantra*), and energy (*utsāha*). The success achieved through these is also threefold; many subdivisions within these have been recorded.
O King, this is indeed the essence of political science (*nīti*); what need is there for further elaboration for you? (86–87)
Having thus deliberated on all this with his ministers, the king,
having attended to his financial affairs at midday, should go to the inner apartments to eat;
he should consume food that has been thoroughly examined and consecrated with mantras that neutralize poison.
Having eaten, he should indeed enjoy himself with the women in the inner apartments (89).
In the afternoon, he should study the Dharmaśāstras and the Purāṇas, after having performed the twilight devotions according to rule and offered oblations into the fire with a concentrated mind (90).

Having eaten and studied the Bhāgavata scripture, he should lie down endowed with meditation, and rise at the proper time, free from fatigue. For a king who conducts himself in this manner and follows the path of political ethics—
Dharma, artha, kāma, and mokṣa shall be accomplished; of this there is no doubt.
(92) Having thus ruled over Pṛthu, Brahmā, the teacher of the worlds, that god, together with the deities, vanished right there. (93)
Vainya also did exactly as that ancient teaching spoken by Brahmā had prescribed; having enjoyed the earth together with its oceans, he eventually entered into Brahman—alas!
O son of Parīkṣit, you too shall attain happiness by acting in this same way.
Having established your fame in the world, you shall attain the supreme goal.
As long as a person's glory circulates among the worlds, for that many thousands of years they are honored in the world of Brahmā. 95–96.
And whoever, being composed, should recite or hear this poem— whether a Brāhmaṇa, a Kṣatriya, especially a king or a ruler of men,
a Vaiśya, one born of the Śūdra caste, or women belonging to the royal household— [shall attain the highest goal]. 97.
Having become renowned in this world, they shall attain their destination in the hereafter.
O Janamejaya, this science of ethics has been proclaimed by me to you;
now, in brief, I shall go where my teacher Vyāsa resides.
Having said "Vaiśampāyana," he departed from that very spot;
and the son of Parīkṣit also rejoiced while protecting his subjects with sound policy.
Thus ends the eighth chapter, titled "The Description of Royal Duties," in the illustrious *Nītiśāstra*, the *Nītiprakāśikā*.
The *Nītiprakāśikā* is completed.
